terms.definition: Numerical values representing one observation. Each coordinate corresponds to an input feature.
A measure of a vector’s length. The Euclidean norm is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates.
The sum of products of corresponding coordinates. It gives a weighted score and relates to the angle between vectors.
Straight-line distance between two points, computed from the squared coordinate differences.
The sum of absolute coordinate differences. It can produce different nearest neighbors from Euclidean distance.
The component of a vector along a chosen direction. It connects geometric alignment to regression and dimensionality reduction.
The surface where a classifier changes its prediction. An affine classifier uses a boundary of the form wᵀx + b = 0.
A row–column dot-product operation. An N by D input matrix multiplied by D by K weights produces N by K scores.
An input-independent offset in a model’s score. It lets an affine decision boundary move away from the origin.
A rule that assigns a quality value to a candidate. State whether the search should minimize or maximize it.
The set of possible candidates. Constraints determine which candidates are valid.
A candidate at least as good as its permitted neighbors, but potentially worse than a distant candidate.
A candidate with the best objective value across the entire feasible search space.
Construction of a solution by choosing the best immediate next part, without generally considering all long-term consequences.
Repeated replacement of a complete candidate by a better neighbor. It can become trapped at a local optimum.
Trying unfamiliar regions of the search space, potentially accepting short-term loss of quality to find better alternatives.
Refining candidates in a promising region using information already found.
Local search that sometimes accepts worse moves. Cooling reduces that acceptance probability and increases exploitation.
Updates that move against the gradient to decrease an objective, or with it to increase one. The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives.
The multiplier controlling the size of a gradient update. Too small can be slow; too large can overshoot or diverge.
Learning a mapping from example inputs to supplied targets, with the aim of making useful predictions on unseen inputs.
Prediction of a numerical target, such as temperature or travel time.
Prediction of a category or label. The meaning of the target determines the task, even when the input features are numbers.
A method that finds the k closest stored examples and aggregates their targets, often by majority vote for classification.
The rule used to decide which inputs are close. Its choice affects neighbor selection and clustering.
Changing feature magnitudes so their units do not unintentionally dominate distances or penalties. Learn scaling statistics from training data only.
A setting chosen outside ordinary parameter fitting, such as k or regularization strength. Select it using validation or cross-validation.
A strategy that stores training examples and performs much of the work at prediction time, as basic kNN does.
Neighbor voting in which closer examples have more influence than distant examples.
A binary classifier that applies a threshold to an affine score and updates its weights when it misclassifies an example.
The existence of one affine hyperplane that correctly separates the training classes.
A Boolean function true when exactly one input is true. Its two positive corners cannot be separated from its negatives by one line.
For 0/1 labels, adding learning_rate × (target − prediction) × input to the weights. Correct predictions cause no update.
A model that predicts a numerical target using an affine combination of input features.
The difference between an observed target and a prediction. Check the sign convention before using it in an update.
The average of squared prediction errors. Squaring prevents positive and negative errors from canceling.
The square root of MSE, expressed in the same units as the target.
The total squared prediction error. On a fixed dataset it has the same minimizing parameters as MSE and RMSE.
Assumptions that restrict the relationships a learner can represent or prefer, such as choosing an affine model.
A stochastic search that evaluates a population and repeatedly applies selection, variation, and replacement.
The encoded candidate manipulated by the algorithm, such as a bit string, real-valued vector, or permutation.
The candidate’s interpreted solution or behavior in the problem being solved.
The quality used to compare candidates and guide evolutionary search. It must reflect the intended task.
A variation operation that changes one candidate, such as flipping a bit or swapping two positions.
Combining information from parents to create offspring. The operation must respect the representation’s validity constraints.
An ordering of distinct items, with each item appearing exactly once. Duplicate entries invalidate a tour encoded this way.
Permutation crossover that preserves a selected segment and uses mappings between parents to repair conflicting outside entries.
Permutation crossover that retains a segment and fills the remaining positions while preserving the other parent’s relative order.
Recombination of real-valued vectors using weighted averages of corresponding entries.
How strongly selection favors high-fitness candidates. Higher pressure can speed improvement but also remove diversity.
Choosing which individuals reproduce. This can use a different rule from selection of the next population.
Choosing which candidates remain in the population after offspring have been generated.
Preserving one or more of the best candidates so variation cannot discard them by chance.
Selection probabilities proportional to suitable nonnegative fitness values. A dominant value can quickly reduce diversity.
Selection based on ordering by fitness rather than its raw magnitude, making pressure less sensitive to scale.
Sampling a group and selecting its best candidate. Larger tournaments generally increase selection pressure.
The degree to which candidates differ. It keeps alternatives available when the current best region is only locally promising.
Reducing effective fitness in crowded regions to encourage the population to occupy several niches.
Making offspring compete mainly with similar individuals, helping preserve different parts of the population.
Real-vector evolutionary search that uses scaled differences between population members to generate trial candidates.
Searching feature subsets by fitting and validating a model for each subset. Selection must respect the training and validation splits.
An affine model with a probability output, commonly sigmoid for binary classification and softmax for exclusive multiclass classification.
A raw score before a sigmoid or softmax converts scores to probabilities.
A function mapping a real score to a value between 0 and 1. A score of zero maps to 0.5.
Normalization of exponentiated logits into a probability distribution over mutually exclusive classes.
A loss penalizing low predicted probability for the observed label. For a one-hot target, it is the negative log of the true-class probability.
A vector with one active entry identifying a category and zero elsewhere. It can encode an exclusive target or index a learned embedding.
Selecting exactly one label from more than two possible classes.
Assigning any applicable subset of labels to an example, often with independent sigmoid outputs.
Fitting one binary classifier per class against all remaining classes, then comparing their outputs.
The cutoff used to turn a probability or score into a label. Changing it trades false alarms against missed positives.
An intermediate set of units transforming inputs into features used by later layers.
A transformation applied to a unit’s pre-activation score. Nonlinear hidden activations let a network express nonlinear relationships.
Computing layer outputs in sequence to obtain a prediction and its loss.
Efficiently computing loss derivatives by applying the chain rule backward through the network.
Computing a derivative through composed operations by combining their local derivatives.
The vector of partial derivatives with respect to parameters. It describes local sensitivity of the objective.
The rule that uses gradients or other information to update parameters. Backpropagation supplies gradients rather than performing the update itself.
A subset of training examples used for one gradient estimate or update. Averaging examples can reduce sampling noise.
Comparing an analytic gradient with a small finite-difference estimate to help find implementation errors.
An existence result for sufficiently wide networks with suitable nonlinear activations. It does not guarantee easy training or generalization.
Performance on unseen examples from the intended task, rather than fit to the training sample alone.
Training fits parameters, validation selects settings, and the final held-out test evaluates the selected procedure.
Held-out information influencing training or model selection, including fitting preprocessing on all data before cross-validation.
Repeated fitting with different held-out folds to compare models or estimate performance.
Restricted models can miss structure through high bias; overly flexible fits can be sensitive to sample noise through high variance.
Counts of true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives for a stated positive class and decision threshold.
The fraction of all examples correctly classified. A majority class can dominate this measure.
The fraction of predicted positives that are truly positive: TP/(TP + FP).
The fraction of actual positives detected: TP/(TP + FN).
The harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is high only when both are sufficiently high.
Giving each class equal weight when combining per-class metric values, regardless of its number of examples.
Plotting true-positive rate against false-positive rate as a classifier’s decision threshold changes.
Plotting precision against recall across decision thresholds, useful for inspecting rare-positive detection.
A summary of a curve over thresholds. AUROC summarizes score ranking, rather than calibration or performance at a specific threshold.
The fraction of actual negatives classified positive: FP/(FP + TN). With many negatives, a small FPR can still mean many false alarms.
The fraction of actual negatives correctly classified: TN/(TN + FP). It equals one minus the false-positive rate.
Constraining a model’s fit through penalties, stopping rules, or other preferences to reduce sensitivity to training-specific detail.
A squared-weight penalty that typically shrinks coefficients without setting many exactly to zero.
An absolute-weight penalty that can set coefficients exactly to zero, selecting a sparse subset of original features.
Combining L1 and L2 penalties to balance sparsity with more stable treatment of correlated features.
Selecting a checkpoint using validation performance before continued fitting worsens generalization.
A training sample drawn with replacement, so some observations repeat and others are omitted.
Fitting models independently on bootstrap samples and averaging or voting. It often reduces variance when their errors differ.
Fitting models sequentially so later rounds respond to earlier errors, then combining their predictions.
Keeping a subset of original input features. Select using only the training side of each evaluation split.
Learning internal feature vectors from data rather than relying entirely on hand-designed input features.
The activation max(0, z). Positive inputs pass through; negative inputs become zero.
Gradient signals shrinking through repeated chain-rule factors, making early layers learn slowly.
Applying learned local filters across input positions. Shared weights reduce parameter count and detect recurring patterns.
Fixed local aggregation, such as a maximum or mean, often reducing spatial size without learned parameters.
Adding a learned transformation to an identity path, making small corrections and gradient propagation easier.
A sequence model updating hidden state from the current input and previous state while sharing weights over time.
A dense vector representation of an item such as a token, often learned jointly with the model.
Generating a sequence one item at a time by feeding chosen outputs into later predictions.
Learning structure or representations from inputs without supplied target labels for the task.
Clustering that alternates nearest-center assignment with mean updates to reduce within-cluster squared distances for a chosen K.
Building nested groups by repeatedly merging clusters, with linkage defining which merge is closest.
A tree recording hierarchical cluster merges. Cutting across higher merges generally gives fewer clusters.
Cluster distances defined by the minimum, maximum, or mean cross-cluster pair distance, respectively.
Merging the pair that gives the smallest increase in within-cluster sum of squared deviations.
Finding orthogonal directions of high variance in centered data and projecting onto selected directions.
Subtracting each feature’s mean. With examples as rows, PCA subtracts column means rather than row means.
The amount of observed variation captured by a component or a set of components, rather than a guarantee of predictive relevance.
A model encoding an input into a representation and decoding it to reconstruct that input.
A low-dimensional visualization method emphasizing local neighbors. Large displayed distances and cluster sizes need not reflect global geometry.
The largest packet size a link can carry without fragmentation at that layer. Encapsulation overhead can reduce the space available to an inner packet.
Splitting an IP packet into fragments. Reassembly needs every fragment, so one missing part prevents delivery of the whole packet.
Finding a usable packet size by reacting to feedback about packets too large for the path. Filtered ICMP can break that feedback.
Using probes and delivery confirmation to discover usable packet sizes without relying solely on ICMP errors.
Sending traffic along several paths to use capacity or improve resilience, potentially introducing reordering.
Keeping packets of a flow on a selected path to reduce reordering. Unequal flow sizes can still make path loads uneven.
Packets arriving in a different order from transmission. A receiver’s gap reports can resemble the signals of loss.
Deployed assumptions and middleboxes making protocol changes difficult, even when endpoints could support them.
The unit exchanged by peer protocol entities, carrying that layer’s control information and payload.
Data handed from an upper layer to a lower layer for transport. The lower layer adds its own protocol information.
Carrying one protocol’s data unit as payload inside another protocol’s unit.
Combining logical flows onto shared resources, then separating received data into the intended flows or applications.
The set of entities cooperating through a layer. Similar functions can recur at hop-local and end-to-end scopes.
Placing functions needing complete application knowledge at endpoints, even when network mechanisms can help performance.
An identifier says which entity is intended; a locator indicates where it can be reached. Combining them complicates mobility.
Routing develops reachability or path information; forwarding uses installed state to choose each packet’s next action.
Maintaining mappings between internal and external addresses or ports so packets can cross addressing realms.
MPTCP presents one logical connection over several TCP subflows. Multiple attachments can provide capacity or resilience but may share bottlenecks.
An ordered reliable byte-stream transport. Applications must define their own message boundaries.
A datagram transport with ports and checksum support, without built-in reliable ordered delivery or congestion control.
Feedback confirming all earlier TCP bytes and naming the next expected byte.
Receiver-advertised capacity limiting outstanding data to protect the receiver from overload.
Negotiating a larger interpretation of TCP’s advertised receive-window value so window limits need not throttle high-bandwidth, high-RTT paths.
Time from sending data or a probe to receiving its corresponding response or acknowledgement.
A timer used to infer loss when expected acknowledgement does not arrive. Its setting must allow for RTT and variation.
Avoiding ambiguous RTT samples after retransmission, when an ACK cannot identify which transmission it acknowledges.
Using duplicate-ACK evidence to recover before a timeout, with congestion responses reflecting that some packets still arrived.
Reporting received blocks beyond a cumulative-ACK gap, helping the sender identify several missing regions.
Loss near the end of a transfer, where too few later packets may trigger fast retransmit. A probe can solicit earlier feedback.
Using delivery acknowledgements and transmission timing to infer losses while allowing a reordering interval.
Adapting a sender’s outstanding data or rate to avoid overloading a shared network path.
Using returning acknowledgements as feedback that data has left the path and more can be sent.
Rapid congestion-window growth while probing capacity, roughly exponential per RTT under the idealized ACK pattern.
Cautious growth combined with proportional backoff after congestion signals, probing capacity while helping competing flows share it.
Bandwidth multiplied by round-trip delay, estimating the data in flight needed to fill a path.
Excessive delay from persistent queues, even when packet loss is low and throughput is high.
Dropping or marking before a queue overflows to signal congestion. RED uses average occupancy; CoDel targets persistent queueing delay.
Combining flow scheduling with per-queue delay control, reducing interference from a single queue-dominating flow.
Marking packets to report congestion without dropping those packets, allowing responsive endpoints to reduce load.
Model-based congestion control estimating bottleneck delivery rate and propagation RTT, with probing needed to refresh those estimates.
Spacing transmissions over time instead of sending large bursts. It complements rather than replaces control of average load.
The way competing traffic shares resources. The result depends on whether the unit is a connection, user, application, or another grouping.
Signal weakening across distance and obstacles, reducing the receiver’s ability to recover information.
Signal power relative to noise power. Together with interference and channel behavior, it affects reliable modulation choices.
Reflected signal copies reaching a receiver over different paths. It can distort signals or provide exploitable spatial diversity.
Encoding information through distinguishable carrier states. A constellation shows possible symbol states and their separation.
Symbols per second versus bits per second. M distinguishable states can encode log₂(M) raw bits per symbol, before coding and overhead.
Separating users into time slots or frequency bands so they can share a medium.
Separating simultaneous transmissions through codes; matching-code correlation recovers a sender in the ideal orthogonal-code model.
Allocating orthogonal subcarriers across time to different users.
Using multiple antennas for spatial diversity or parallel streams, depending on channel conditions.
Combining antenna signals to reinforce transmission or reception in selected directions.
Use of high-frequency bands that can provide wide bandwidth but often need careful beam alignment and handling of blockage.
Connecting a wireless client to an access point and its basic service set before using the network through it.
Checking for local channel activity before transmitting. Hidden senders and propagation delay mean collisions remain possible.
A transmitter unable to hear another transmitter that can interfere at the same receiver.
Waiting a randomized interval before retrying access, reducing repeated simultaneous transmissions.
Short reservation exchanges that can reduce costly data collisions but consume airtime themselves.
Changing transmission settings as radio conditions change, trading raw rate against errors and retransmission overhead.
Control functions establish and manage state; the data plane carries user packets using that state.
Changing the serving radio access point or base station while maintaining connectivity where supported.
Routing a visitor’s traffic through its home operator, providing control and accounting at a potential RTT cost.
Allowing roaming traffic to exit through the visited network rather than taking a home-network detour.
An operator selling mobile service using another operator’s radio resources, with varying ownership of core-network functions.
Many low-cost devices exchanging small amounts of data, often prioritizing battery life, coverage, and scale over peak throughput.
A network designed for low-rate communication across wide areas with energy-constrained devices.
LoRa is the radio modulation; LoRaWAN defines networking and medium-access behavior around it, typically using shared unlicensed spectrum.
A LoRa setting increasing symbol duration and potential reception robustness at the cost of longer airtime.
Adjusting radio settings such as rate and power to match link conditions and reduce unnecessary airtime or energy use.
A cellular IoT technology using narrowband radio resources and operator infrastructure, with mechanisms for coverage enhancement and power saving.
Using mechanisms such as repeated transmissions and concentrated power to improve reception, with time and energy costs.
Allowing a registered device to sleep without continuous receiver availability, delaying network-initiated communication until it wakes.
Spacing receiver listening opportunities farther apart to save energy, at the cost of downlink latency.
Using shared infrastructure to provide logically differentiated services with different resource and isolation requirements.
Reusing an established connection across requests, avoiding repeated setup and allowing transport state to carry forward.
Encoding messages as smaller structured frames that endpoints can identify and reassemble.
A stream is a logical bidirectional channel; a message carries a request or response; frames are the smaller units used to encode it.
Interleaving frames from different logical streams over one connection, identified by stream IDs.
Later data waiting behind an earlier unresolved item. HTTP/2 avoids response-order serialization but still inherits TCP’s ordered-byte-stream gaps.
Providing relative scheduling preferences for streams when resources are limited; actual behavior depends on endpoints and policy.
Reducing HTTP/2 metadata by using compact representations and indexes for repeated header fields.
A transport over UDP integrating reliable streams, flow and congestion control, loss recovery, and a TLS 1.3 handshake.
HTTP using QUIC streams instead of TCP as its transport.
A fresh QUIC connection normally uses a handshake RTT; suitable resumption state can permit early data in the first flight.
QUIC identifiers that associate packets with a logical connection across address changes, subject to path validation.
Identifiers unique to packet transmissions, helping acknowledgements distinguish retransmitted information and improve RTT measurement.
Renting infrastructure while managing operating systems and applications yourself.
Deploying applications onto a provider-managed platform and runtime.
Using a provider-managed application, with less responsibility for its underlying stack.
The ability to handle increasing workload by using suitable additional resources or capacity.
Dynamically adding and removing resources as demand changes, rather than relying solely on fixed provisioning.
Presenting logical execution environments on shared physical hardware, with a hypervisor managing VM resources and isolation.
Sharing infrastructure or a service among customers while separating their data, configuration, and resource use.
Availability concerns usable service; reliability concerns correct operation over time; resilience concerns maintaining or recovering service through disruptions.
A contract describing measurable service commitments, such as uptime or response time, and how failures are handled.
Deployment models differing in access and ownership. Hybrid arrangements connect distinct cloud environments.
Distributing work across resources to reduce overload and use capacity, subject to downstream bottlenecks.
Plans and recoverable copies for restoring service or data after disruption. This serves a different purpose from live failover alone.
Forwarding packets using labels and installed mappings, separating forwarding operations from path and service decisions.
Packets grouped for the same forwarding treatment, such as a destination, service, or engineered path.
The path followed through an MPLS domain using label-based forwarding.
Adding a label, replacing the top label during forwarding, and removing a label.
Exchanging label bindings used to build MPLS forwarding state, following routing reachability in the lecture’s basic example.
Choosing paths using constraints and capacity needs rather than relying only on ordinary destination-based least cost.
Using a prepared local detour around a failure while broader control-plane recovery proceeds.
Multiple labels with different roles, such as an outer transport label and an inner VPN or service label.
Separate routing contexts supporting customer-specific IP connectivity over shared infrastructure.
Emulating link-layer connectivity over a provider network, using labels to identify the transported service.
Preventing buffer overflow under the design’s assumptions by limiting injection. It does not eliminate congestion or all possible losses.
Sending only when credits indicate reserved receiver buffer capacity; returning credits permits further transmission.
Stop/go feedback that pauses a sender before buffers overflow and resumes it when space becomes available.
Time to put packet bits onto a link versus time for the signal to travel along it.
The capacity across a minimum-bandwidth cut dividing a network into roughly equal halves.
A switching fabric able to connect nonconflicting input–output pairs, with hardware cost growing rapidly with port count.
Direct networks distribute attached endpoints among switches; indirect networks connect endpoints through a fabric of intermediate switches.
Waiting for a busy resource. A structurally blocking fabric can force otherwise independent transfers to share an internal path.
A set of packets unable to progress because each waits for resources held by another in a dependency cycle.
Packets continuing to move without reaching their destination.
Restricting routes to an ordered sequence of dimensions, preventing cyclic channel dependencies on suitable mesh designs.
Separately managed logical buffering and flow-control resources over a physical channel, useful for managing dependencies or traffic classes.
The access network attaches devices; distribution aggregates their connectivity toward gateways and upstream links.
The router a host uses to reach destinations outside its directly connected network.
Duplicate resources or paths intended to preserve service when something fails.
A component or dependency whose failure can stop the service despite other functioning resources.
A dependency such as power, location, or conduit that can disable several supposedly independent components together.
Selecting a loop-free active layer-2 topology while redundant physical links exist.
Maintaining a usable default gateway when one router fails, protecting a different function from layer-2 loop prevention.
Spare capacity needed to absorb redirected traffic after failure, rather than merely providing an alternative path.
Carrying different optical channels on separate wavelengths over shared fiber.
Power-resilience resources covering different timescales, with their independence and transfer behavior affecting service continuity.
